question.problem:
Solve the initial value problem
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118512/assets/be4b1ac82a25533e28028ad0aade71e2dd2614c5cd302d777a90a9f16be845c1.svg)
*Hint: The only eigenvalue of the system's matrix is $\lambda=3.$*
question.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118512/assets/dfddfc4e82f21cd490aff75bbdc6fbece98cd05a5cc70a1148492697faa8741a.svg)

We are given that the eigenvalue is $\lambda=3$ (of multiplicity two). For this eigenvalue, we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118512/assets/92c6c6be816658e065ebba1079a2c7fa031cc9137ffa8dec7bf6e498e69195f3.svg)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118512/assets/75524e426e894f50985740367c96f128dfef1e216ae6969a529889cf22803bc7.svg)

Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda$ and only one linearly independent eigenvector $\mathbf v,$ the solution to the system of differential equations is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1  \mathbf{v}e^{\lambda t} + c_2 (\mathbf{v}t e^{\lambda t} +  \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t}),
$$

where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

To find $\mathbf{w},$ we solve the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-\lambda I)w & =v \\ [\begin{aligned}-1-3 & -8 \\ 2 & 7-3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-4 & -8 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{w}_{1} \\ {w}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The last equality allows us to form the following system of equations:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118512/assets/bb892c2fd7b1a2873b9a7427d95599f67fbd10e47ec6fd2cb377b9f6f45f4185.svg)

Note that the first equation is a constant multiple of the second. So, we obtain

$$
w_1 =\dfrac{1}{2} - 2 w_2 .
$$

The variable $w_2$ is a free variable. Setting $w_2 = 0,$  we get $w_1 = \dfrac{1}{2},$ and therefore
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118512/assets/4696fe4ee3fd46a639fb465c10aa2ac44e608a0cf59ca6c1a210eb4861b3dd5b.svg)

Therefore, the general solution is given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118512/assets/0525d47967c203832ff4deea0931e007cc7127f24d248cd8265765ad95708367.svg)

Now, we need to find the values of $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial condition ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118512/assets/48da1d81a447aa78c3ffa68ad5f089bc0d8e4bac5fa489ddad2747055b0f2a99.svg) Substituting $t=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(0) & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to our initial value problem is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{x}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}-2([\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]t{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]t{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(4t-3){e}^{3t} \\ (1-2t){e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
